analysis.one_liner: Taxes away, dollar for dollar, the windfall profits of wholesale electricity sellers in the West.
analysis.headline: A bill to strip 100% of the excess profits earned by Western wholesale power sellers was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in February 2001 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action.
analysis.plain_summary: During the Western electricity crisis, power sellers charged far more than the cost-based rates allowed under the Federal Power Act. This bill would impose a 100% excise tax on every dollar of that excess profit, effective back to June 1, 2000, with the sellers themselves paying. The goal was to claw back the windfall that wholesalers made while Western customers paid soaring electric bills. The bill went to the House Ways and Means Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Electricity customers across the Western power grid, who were paying prices driven up by sellers charging above cost-based rates; the tax would have recaptured those excess profits for the Treasury rather than leaving them with the sellers.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes an excise tax equal to 100% of the 'windfall profit' from wholesale electricity sales in the Western System Coordinating Council, defining windfall profit as the amount by which the sale price exceeds cost-based rates set under the Federal Power Act, including a fair return on invested capital.
Makes the seller of the electricity liable for the tax, so the excess profit is recaptured rather than passed to buyers.
Applies retroactively to electricity sold after June 1, 2000, covering the period of the Western power crisis.

analysis.who_pays: Wholesale electricity sellers — merchant generators and power marketers in the Western grid — who would surrender every dollar earned above cost-based rates, effective back to mid-2000.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wholesale power generators in the West

drawbacks.text: A 100% tax on anything earned above cost-of-service rates would sharply reduce any incentive to sell extra power into the wholesale market during a shortage, and an honest supporter would have to acknowledge it could discourage the very supply the crisis needed.

The tax reaches back to sales after June 1, 2000, meaning sellers would owe the tax on transactions completed before the bill existed — a retroactive application that is a standard objection to windfall-profit taxes.
It offers no relief mechanism for consumers facing bills immediately; it recaptures revenue for the Treasury rather than directly lowering customers' rates.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If the goal was to stop sellers from profiting above cost-based rates during the Western crisis, the bill did that bluntly and completely — every dollar of excess profit taxed away. The honest trade-offs are real: a 100% rate gives sellers no reason to bring marginal supply to market in a shortage, and the retroactive reach raises fairness concerns for sellers who priced under the rules then in force. A more carefully designed version might have capped the rate or applied prospectively; this bill chose simplicity and severity.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and sat there for the rest of the Congress — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Bob Filner introduced the bill on February 6, 2001, during the aftermath of the Western electricity price spike.
Two House Democrats cosponsored it; no other support is recorded.
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee, which took no further action for the remainder of the 107th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wholesale electricity sellers kept the excess profits they had earned above cost-based rates during the Western crisis, because the tax that would have recaptured them never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wholesale power sellers kept their excess profits

for.name: Rep. Bob Filner
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to impose a 100% windfall-profit tax on Western wholesale electricity sales.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no report — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only three House Democrats sponsored or cosponsored the bill; no Republicans took a recorded position and no vote ever occurred, so no partisan split is visible in the record.

industries.industry: Wholesale electricity generators and power marketers
industries.note: The bill would have taken 100% of the profit they earned selling power above cost-based rates in the Western grid, retroactive to June 2000. Those excess profits came directly out of the bills Western electricity customers were paying during the crisis.
